distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for the full clinical spectrum of typhoid fever.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Exposure to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi through contaminated food or water, close contact with a case or carrier, endemic residence, or travel. This changes disease prior and incubation timing but is not by itself a severity marker.

Organisms cross terminal ileal mucosa through M cells and invade Peyer patches, producing abdominal pain, diarrhea or constipation, nausea/vomiting, ileitis, bowel-wall thickening, and early mesenteric lymph-node involvement.

Typhi survives in macrophages and reticuloendothelial organs, explaining sustained fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, relapse risk, and need for adequate intracellular-active or long-duration therapy.

Viable Salmonella Typhi circulates from intestinal and reticuloendothelial reservoirs. Bacteremia may be intermittent or low density but is the substrate for systemic inflammation, complications, and microbiologic diagnosis.

Innate response to intracellular gram-negative infection drives sustained fever, headache, malaise, relative bradycardia in some patients, rose spots, CRP elevation, hepatic enzyme elevation, and severe inflammatory shock in a minority.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Bone marrow and leukocyte response suppression
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Marrow involvement and cytokine-mediated suppression produce normal or low WBC counts, leukopenia, eosinopenia, mild thrombocytopenia, and anemia in some patients rather than the neutrophilic pattern typical of pyogenic sepsis.
Liver and spleen involvement causes hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, mild jaundice or bilirubin elevation, transaminitis, hypoalbuminemia, and sometimes gallbladder involvement.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Peyer patch necrosis and intestinal ulceration
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Second-to-third week necrosis of infected lymphoid tissue in terminal ileum and adjacent bowel produces intestinal ulcers, lower GI bleeding, perforation, peritonitis, and need for urgent source control.

Systemic inflammation, endotoxemia, hepatic dysfunction, metabolic derangement, and rarely direct CNS involvement produce delirium, obtundation, psychosis, meningitis-like CSF inflammation, cranial neuropathy, or seizures.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Septic shock, capillary leak, and ARDS pathway
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Severe typhoid can trigger distributive shock, coagulopathy, diffuse capillary leak, pleural effusions, ascites, pulmonary infiltrates, and acute respiratory distress syndrome.

Fluoroquinolone resistance, MDR, XDR, ESBL plasmids, inadequate intracellular activity, short duration, or delayed active therapy prolong bacteremia and intracellular persistence, increasing relapse and complication risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Biliary seeding and chronic carriage pathway
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Persistence in gallbladder biofilm or biliary disease can create prolonged fecal shedding, relapse, or chronic carrier state, especially with gallstones or structural biliary disease.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: After ingestion, Typhi invades ileal mucosa following an incubation period.
Mucosal invasion seeds macrophages and reticuloendothelial tissues.
Intracellular reservoirs periodically release organisms into blood.
Circulating and tissue organisms drive innate inflammatory response.
Reticuloendothelial infection localizes in liver and spleen.
Marrow involvement and inflammatory suppression produce cytopenias.
Persistent lymphoid infection in terminal ileum can progress to necrosis and ulceration.
Cytokine and endotoxin effects contribute to delirium, obtundation, and encephalopathy.
Severe inflammatory response can produce distributive shock and capillary leak.
Inactive or clinically weak therapy prolongs viable organism burden.
Poor intracellular killing and resistance allow dormant reservoirs to persist.
Organisms may seed the gallbladder and persist in biofilm or biliary disease.
Travel, endemic residence, unsafe food or water, or close contact are direct exposure context.
Many cases occur after exposure in endemic regions or travel from them.
Ileitis and mesenteric lymphadenitis cause abdominal pain.
Enteritis commonly causes diarrhea, sometimes alternating with constipation.
Constipation is a classic early gastrointestinal pattern in some patients.
Ileitis and enteritis can appear as bowel-wall thickening, ileal inflammation, ascites, or ulcers.
Sustained fever is the core systemic manifestation.
History often shows several days to weeks of continuous fever.
Headache and malaise are common cytokine symptoms.
Malaise and fatigue track systemic inflammation and prolonged fever.
Relative bradycardia can occur despite high fever, although it is neither universal nor specific.
Rose spots are sparse salmon-colored macules from bacteremic/inflammatory skin involvement.
CRP is often moderately to markedly elevated.
Normal WBC or leukopenia is common and contrasts with many pyogenic infections.
Marrow suppression can lower neutrophil count or blunt neutrophilia.
Eosinopenia or aneosinophilia is a recognized laboratory clue.
Mild to moderate thrombocytopenia occurs with marrow suppression, splenic sequestration, or severe infection.
Liver involvement can produce palpable hepatomegaly.
Splenic reticuloendothelial involvement produces splenomegaly.
Transaminitis is common during systemic typhoid fever.
ALT often rises as hepatic involvement becomes evident.
Jaundice or bilirubin elevation occurs in hepatic or severe disease.
Typhi bacteremia is a gram-negative bacteremia context; culture/speciation should remain confirmatory evidence.
Blood culture positivity is most likely early and declines after antibiotics or later disease.
Peyer patch necrosis creates intestinal ulceration.
Ulcerated ileal lesions can bleed, producing melena or hematochezia.
Deep necrotic ulcers can perforate terminal ileum or adjacent bowel.
Typhoid encephalopathy manifests as delirium, disorientation, obtundation, or psychosis.
Worsening neurotoxicity increases encephalopathy event risk.
Distributive shock and capillary leak lower MAP unless rescued by fluids or vasopressors.
Severe typhoid can progress to septic shock.
Severe capillary leak and inflammatory lung injury can produce ARDS.
XDR is a pathogen-context axis that blocks several usual antibiotic paths.
Resistance and inactive empiric therapy reduce the probability that current antibiotics cover the organism.
Initial inactive antibiotics are a common observed expression of resistance or wrong empiric choice.
Gallbladder persistence creates chronic carriage and shedding.
Residual intracellular or lymph-node organisms can reactivate after apparent recovery.
Perforation, peritonitis, and major GI bleeding increase lifespan hazard.
Shock and ARDS are direct high-mortality pathways.
Obtundation and encephalopathy mark severe systemic disease and aspiration/ICU risk.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever usually increases heart rate, but typhoid can show relative bradycardia; dehydration, shock, pain, and ARDS restore tachycardia.
Relative bradycardia lowers observed heart rate relative to fever-predicted heart rate.
More intense ileitis/enteritis increases abdominal pain and tenderness.
Deep intestinal ulcers increase the hazard of melena, hematochezia, or major lower GI bleeding.
Deep necrotic ulcers can progress to ileal or ileocecal perforation.
Perforation produces peritoneal contamination, guarding, rigidity, free air, and sepsis physiology.
Peritonitis from bowel perforation generally requires urgent surgical source control.
Adequate control of perforation, bleeding, or focal complications reduces mortality hazard.
Shock is a direct high-mortality pathway.
ARDS adds respiratory failure and ICU-level mortality risk.
Severe neurologic involvement signals systemic severity and aspiration/ICU risk.
Adequate active therapy lowers persistence and relapse risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ceftriaxone requires isolate susceptibility to lower viable Typhi burden.
XDR Typhi is often resistant to third-generation cephalosporins.
Severe beta-lactam reactions constrain cephalosporin use.
Antibiotics alone do not control perforation and fecal peritonitis.

failure_modes: persistent intracellular reservoir with too-short duration
unrecognized perforation or bleeding requiring source control

side_effects.interpretation: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea can confuse symptom tracking.
Rare hepatobiliary intolerance or biliary sludge signal.

treatments.context_specific_role: Parenteral beta-lactam path when cephalosporin susceptibility and patient allergy context support use.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Macrolide activity depends on isolate susceptibility and adequate exposure.
Vomiting, severe enteritis, ileus, or NPO status can prevent reliable oral therapy.
Azithromycin accumulates intracellularly and can help when intracellular persistence is prominent.

failure_modes: unreliable oral absorption or persistent vomiting
severe shock or perforation where oral-only therapy is inadequate

side_effects.interpretation: Macrolide GI intolerance can reduce absorption.

treatments.context_specific_role: Intracellular-active oral or IV-compatible path when susceptibility and absorption context are favorable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluoroquinolone resistance is common in many acquisition regions and strongly reduces effect.
Pregnancy changes safety and treatment selection.
XDR Typhi includes fluoroquinolone resistance.

failure_modes: pregnancy or safety context prevents use
severe vomiting or poor absorption if oral route is used
treatments.context_specific_role: High-intracellular-penetration path when fluoroquinolone susceptibility is credible and safety context permits.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Carbapenem effect requires isolate susceptibility.
XDR may leave carbapenems among the few parenteral active options.
Clinical response can be slow or incomplete when intracellular persistence dominates despite in vitro susceptibility.
Dose adjustment is required to avoid neurotoxicity and maintain exposure.

failure_modes: intracellular persistence or tolerance with delayed clinical response
monotherapy in severe persistent disease despite susceptibility

side_effects.interpretation: Beta-lactam neurotoxicity risk rises with renal impairment.

treatments.context_specific_role: Parenteral active-coverage path for cephalosporin-resistant or severe resistant typhoid, with explicit risk of incomplete intracellular clearance.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Combination pairs extracellular/bacteremia activity with intracellular-active macrolide exposure.
If ceftriaxone is inactive, the beta-lactam component adds little.
Vomiting or NPO status may require IV-compatible therapy.

failure_modes: ceftriaxone-resistant XDR isolate with no active beta-lactam contribution
azithromycin resistance or unreliable enteral absorption

side_effects.interpretation: Macrolide GI intolerance can reduce effective exposure.

treatments.context_specific_role: Combination path when intracellular persistence, severe disease, or relapse concern makes single-path suppression less reliable and susceptibility context supports both components.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Aminopenicillins are only useful if susceptibility is retained.
XDR phenotype includes resistance to older first-line agents.
Severe beta-lactam allergy constrains use.

failure_modes: unreliable oral absorption if oral step-down is used

side_effects.interpretation: Drug eruption can mimic disease rash.

treatments.context_specific_role: Susceptibility-dependent beta-lactam path for selected isolates or step-down contexts.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TMP-SMX requires retained susceptibility.
Pregnancy changes safety and folate-related risk assessment.
Renal impairment increases hyperkalemia and drug accumulation risk.

failure_modes: pregnancy or renal/toxicity context limits use

side_effects.interpretation: TMP component can raise potassium, especially with renal impairment.
Rare marrow toxicity can worsen leukopenia.

treatments.context_specific_role: Susceptibility-dependent oral or adjunct path where safety context allows.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Activity requires retained susceptibility.
Existing cytopenia raises marrow-toxicity concern.

side_effects.interpretation: Reversible marrow suppression or rare aplastic anemia signal.

treatments.context_specific_role: Susceptibility-dependent historical intracellular-active path, constrained by toxicity and availability.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Surgery only helps when there is a perforation/peritonitis or other controllable source.
Incomplete lavage, repair, resection, or drainage leaves ongoing contamination.
Shock increases operative risk but does not remove the need for source control when perforation is present.

failure_modes: anastomotic leak, fecal fistula, or ongoing contamination
antibiotic therapy not continued after source control

side_effects.interpretation: Operative bleeding risk in coagulopathy or shock.

treatments.context_specific_role: Procedural path for perforation/peritonitis or uncontrolled intra-abdominal source, bundled with antibiotics and resuscitation.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Adjunct corticosteroid effect is mainly relevant in severe neurologic or shock presentations.
Severe shock is a context where cytokine suppression may improve trajectory in selected reports.
Steroids can worsen bleeding risk and usually require gastric protection when used.
Immunosuppression without active antimicrobial therapy is unsafe.

failure_modes: GI bleeding or perforation risk not controlled
hyperglycemia or secondary infection in prolonged courses

side_effects.interpretation: Steroids can increase GI bleeding risk, especially with mucosal ulceration.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct anti-inflammatory path for selected severe shock, ARDS, or encephalopathy contexts after active antimicrobial therapy and bleeding/perforation risk assessment.

exposure_prior.trajectory_modulation: Raises pre-test probability when prolonged fever, GI symptoms, leukopenia, or transaminitis follows travel or residence in an endemic region.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Typhoid remains strongly geography- and sanitation-linked.

exposure_prior.trajectory_modulation: Supports fecal-oral inoculation and GI-dominant onset.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Contaminated food or water is the main transmission route.

exposure_prior_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Partially lowers probability and severe disease risk but does not exclude typhoid.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Vaccination is incomplete protection and wanes over time.

disease_course_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Prolongs bacteremia, increases ulceration/perforation and relapse hazard, and can make presentation more complicated.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Inactive therapy allows persistent organisms and delays clinical improvement.
Relapse is more likely after inadequate intracellular clearance or short/weak therapy.
Untreated second-to-third week disease increases ulceration and perforation risk.

pathogen_context_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Resistance does not define a separate first-layer disease leaf; it reshapes treatment effect and persistence.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Travel/residence in regions with XDR outbreaks or known resistant isolate increases XDR probability.
Resistance lowers empiric active-coverage probability until susceptibility is known.

host_risk_context.trajectory_modulation: Pregnancy changes severity tolerance, dehydration risk, fetal risk, and antibiotic usability rather than defining a separate manifold.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Pregnancy is a treatment-context and risk-context axis.
Vomiting and poor oral intake in pregnancy can make oral therapy less reliable.

host_risk_context.trajectory_modulation: Increases risk of complications, blunted inflammatory response, bacteremia persistence, and mortality.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Poor physiologic reserve increases hazard once severe typhoid develops.
Host reserve can blunt leukocyte response.

relapse_carrier_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Raises chronic carriage, relapse, and focal biliary persistence risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Gallstones and biliary biofilm favor chronic carrier state.
Persistent biliary reservoirs can reseed infection.

supportive_care: Record travel, migration, food/water, sanitation, household contact, vaccination, and outbreak exposure history explicitly.
Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible, but do not delay active therapy in severe disease.
Keep Salmonella Typhi culture/speciation, Widal, PCR, and susceptibility results as confirmatory or treatment-context evidence rather than ordinary presentation observations.
Monitor CBC with differential, platelets, AST/ALT, bilirubin, albumin, creatinine, electrolytes, CRP, and coagulation studies in hospitalized or complicated disease.
Use hydration, electrolyte correction, antipyretics, nutrition support, antiemetics, and careful oral-intake assessment while antimicrobial therapy takes effect.
Assess for intestinal bleeding or perforation when abdominal pain worsens, peritonitis appears, hemoglobin falls, melena/hematochezia occurs, or free air/ascites is seen.
Use urgent surgical consultation and source control for perforation, fecal peritonitis, uncontrolled bleeding, abscess, or selected biliary carrier/cholecystitis contexts.
Escalate to ICU-level care for shock, ARDS, severe encephalopathy, vasopressor need, mechanical ventilation, or rapidly progressive capillary leak.
Use antimicrobial susceptibility and acquisition geography to update active coverage, XDR probability, and relapse risk instead of hardcoding a single drug order.
After treatment, document clinical response, stool shedding when relevant, relapse symptoms, and public health notification/contact precautions according to local requirements.
quality_notes: This leaf is Typhoid fever only. Paratyphoid fever, XDR typhoid, perforated typhoid, and carrier state are represented as axes, risk/context modifiers, or complications rather than separate IDs here.
There is exactly one derived_hazard axis: mortality_hazard_in_D-TYPHOID-FEVER.
Antimicrobial resistance and susceptibility are treatment-context axes because they are not reliably inferable from routine vitals and labs.
